ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
The solutions in the two arms of this U-tube are separated by a membrane that is permeable to water and sodium chloride, but not to sucrose. Side A is filled with a solution of 0.6 M sucrose and 0.2 M sodium chloride (NaCl), and side B is filled with a solution of 0.2 M sucrose and 0.3 M NaCl. Initially, the volume on both sides is the same.

If you examine side A after a couple of days, you will see
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text: an increase in the concentration of NaCl and an increase in the water level.

ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: The solutions in the two arms of this U-tube are separated by a membrane that is permeable to water and sodium chloride, but not to sucrose. Side A is filled with a solution of 0.6 M sucrose and 0.2 M sodium chloride (NaCl), and side B is filled with a solution of 0.2 M sucrose and 0.3 M NaCl. Initially, the volume on both sides is the same. After a couple of days, what happens to the concentration of NaCl on side A?
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The diagram shows a U-tube with Side A on the left and Side B on the right, separated at the bottom by a membrane. Side A is labeled 0.6 M sucrose and 0.2 M NaCl. Side B is labeled 0.2 M sucrose and 0.3 M NaCl. The membrane is stated to be permeable to water and sodium chloride, but not to sucrose. Reasoning: Since NaCl can pass through the membrane, it can redistribute between the two sides. Initially, Side A has 0.2 M NaCl, while Side B has 0.3 M NaCl. NaCl therefore diffuses from the higher-concentration side, Side B, toward the lower-concentration side, Side A. With initially equal volumes, the NaCl concentration tends toward an intermediate value, about 0.25 M, which is higher than Side A’s starting 0.2 M. Therefore, the concentration of NaCl on Side A increases.
